title: Distributed Message Queue
oneLine: Partition an append-only log, replicate each partition with a leader and followers, let consumer groups own partitions, and make semantics explicit through offsets and idempotency.
opening: I would model each topic as multiple ordered partitions. Producers select a partition by key when per-entity ordering is required, or round-robin for balance. The partition leader appends batches to immutable log segments and replicates to followers; acknowledgment policy trades latency against durability. Consumers pull, maintain offsets, and join groups where each partition is owned by at most one consumer in a group, giving parallelism while preserving order within that partition. A coordinator manages heartbeats and rebalances. Metadata and leader epochs live in a consensus-backed control plane. The service is naturally at-least-once; exactly-once business effects require idempotent producers, transactional offset/output commits where supported, and an idempotent or transactional sink. Retention and replay are first-class, unlike a transient task queue.
ask: Task queue, pub/sub log, or both?
What ordering scope and delivery semantics are required?
Throughput, partitions, regions, and acceptable data loss/latency?
scale: Partition count sets maximum ordered-consumer parallelism; changing it can alter key-to-partition mapping.
Batch size improves throughput but adds latency and memory pressure.
Disk bandwidth and page cache are usually more important than random IOPS because writes/reads are sequential.

decisions.default: Key by entity when ordering matters; otherwise balanced round-robin/sticky batches.
decisions.why: Ordering exists only within a partition and hot keys can cap throughput.
decisions.switch: Use more granular subkeys plus downstream reconciliation when one entity is too hot.

decisions.default: ACK after leader plus sufficient in-sync replicas for durable business events.
decisions.why: Leader-only ACK can lose acknowledged data on failover.
decisions.switch: ACK leader or no ACK for telemetry where small loss is acceptable and latency dominates.

decisions.default: At-least-once with idempotent processing and explicit offset ownership.
decisions.why: Crashes between side effect and offset commit cause redelivery.
decisions.switch: At-most-once for expendable metrics; transactional consume-transform-produce where broker supports it.

decisions.default: Consumer pull with long polling and byte/count limits.
decisions.why: Consumers control pace and backpressure; batching is efficient.
decisions.switch: Push gateways can adapt a log to webhook clients but must preserve retry/flow control.

deepDives.title: Log storage
points: Append immutable records to segment files with sparse indexes and checksums.
Delete or compact whole segments by retention/compaction policy.
Use zero-copy/page cache and sequential batch I/O for throughput.

deepDives.title: Rebalance
points: Heartbeats detect failed consumers; coordinator advances group generation and reassigns partitions.
Fence old owners so two consumers cannot commit the same partition generation.

deepDives.title: Exactly-once nuance
points: Idempotent producer prevents duplicate appends from retries.
Broker transaction can atomically commit produced records and consumed offsets inside the broker.
External DB/API side effects still need idempotency, outbox/inbox, or a transaction bridge.

deepDives.title: Delayed/retry messages
points: Do not repeatedly block a hot ordered partition on one poison record.
Use retry topics/time buckets or a timing wheel and preserve original key/attempt metadata.
Define when ordering is more important than progress.

failures.response: Elect only an in-sync follower, use leader epochs, truncate divergent tails, and choose unclean election policy explicitly.
Idempotency key/inbox table, transactional sink, and commit offset only after durable business effect.
Better key distribution, isolate hot entity, split workload semantics, and monitor per-partition bytes/lag.

failures.risk: Disk fills or consumer falls behind retention
failures.response: Quotas, tiered storage, lag alerts, backpressure, and an explicit reset/recovery workflow.

questions.a: Existing records remain ordered within old partitions, but a hash modulo partition count may route the same key to a new partition. Use stable partition mapping, key-range migration, or accept a cutover epoch.

questions.q: What does exactly once mean here?
questions.a: Be explicit about boundary. The broker can avoid duplicate records and atomically move offsets with output, but an external payment or database write still needs its own idempotency or transaction design.

questions.q: Why does Kafka-like storage retain messages after consumption?
questions.a: Consumer progress is an offset, not record deletion. Independent groups can replay at their own pace, and retention is time/size/compaction based.

questions.q: How do you choose partition count?
questions.a: From peak throughput per partition, desired consumer parallelism, future growth, and metadata/recovery cost. Overpartition modestly, but thousands of tiny partitions also have operational cost.

mistakes: Calling broker transactions end-to-end exactly once
Committing offset before side effect for at-least-once workflows
Ignoring consumer lag and retention exhaustion
seniorSignal: Define ordering and exactly-once boundaries precisely. Discuss leader epochs, rebalances, fencing, hot partitions, retention, and sink idempotency—not only Kafka terminology.
implementation: Kafka/Pulsar concepts: append logs, partitions, ISR, groups, offsets
Spring Kafka with idempotent producer and manual/transactional offset control
Inbox/outbox tables for external database effects
Per-partition lag, under-replicated partition, disk, and rebalance telemetry
